basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan's average farmer age ~64 (official avg rose 53.4 in 2005 to 58.4 by 2020, DGBAS); agricultural workforce fell from ~1.55M (1978) to ~530,000 (2022), an ~66% drop, 80%+ now middle-aged/elderly (農傳媒, DGBAS census); YesHealth Group / 源鮮智慧農場 R&D team 2008, founded 2013, Taoyuan hydroponic plant factory, exported whole-farm tech to Shenzhen (2018), Denmark (2019), reached Vatican, combined daily output 4,400+ kg, WEF Technology Pioneer (company site, business press); NYCU 5G smart farm — real-time AI/5G soil sensors, year-round white strawberries, turmeric curcumin up 3-4x; Tainan City + 經緯航太科技 AI photo-based disease ID across 10 crop types; NTU Bio-Industrial Mechatronics orchid disease-recognition robot; Academia Sinica Agricultural Biotechnology Research Center (ABRC) — stress-tolerance (drought/disease/salinity) crop gene research, described only in general terms, no specific gene/variety invented; World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg), Tainan, founded 1971 as Asian Vegetable Research and Development Center (AVRDC) by Taiwan/US/Japan/Korea/Thailand/Philippines/South Vietnam + ADB, renamed 2008; grouper (石斑魚) aquaculture #1 world production value/#2 volume (2008 FAO), 30+ yrs breeding history, AIoT ponds monitor O2/temp/pH, Fisheries Agency's first onshore leopard coral grouper (東星斑) farming; plant-factory lighting ~50% setup cost, electricity ~1/3 running cost (up to 27% per Japanese estimate), un-subsidised indoor produce often costs more than field-grown, sector fragmented; Taiwan bans domestic GMO cultivation but allows labelled GMO feed/grain imports; grouper-farming know-how leaked to China competitors, Taiwan grouper export value fell ~NT$2.9-3 billion (TVBS, 台灣光華雜誌). "ASIAGA" named in the task brief could not be verified as a distinct real entity; the closest verified real institute matching that description is the World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg/AVRDC), Tainan — used instead. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: Imagine a leafy plant growing inside a sealed building with no windows and no daylight, kept alive under pink LED bulbs that never switch off. Does that honestly still count as farming?
slides.2: SDG 2 demands farming that can bounce back from real disasters and keep going, which brings us to today's actual question. Can new machines take the place of Taiwan's fading farmers?
slides.3: By now, the typical farmer is roughly 64 years old, and that number keeps climbing. What we're discussing here is a fading workforce, not simply a food shortage.
slides.4: Taiwan's farming workforce has shrunk a great deal since 1978. It fell from about 1.55 million workers to just 530,000 by 2022. Most people still working are now middle-aged or older.
slides.5: Farming remains physically tough with disappointing pay next to city jobs, so most young people won't take it on. That's why so much land now sits unused or gets rented to strangers.
slides.6: Here's an uncomfortable thought worth pausing on. If we don't find new workers or genuinely better tools, who will be growing our food, or catching our fish, twenty years ahead?
slides.7: Genuine success stories are already emerging here. YesHealth, a local company, built a massive indoor facility in Taoyuan. It has since shipped its whole growing setup overseas, to Shenzhen, Denmark and the Vatican.
slides.8: Sensor tech is quietly reshaping how farms work too, though few people have actually noticed yet. One university's farm now relies on 5G and AI. It grows strawberries beyond their usual season while boosting turmeric's value.
slides.9: Aquaculture has transformed quite a bit too. Taiwan has long led the world in breeding grouper fish. Water sensors have recently made it possible to farm a brand new grouper species on land.
slides.10: Rather than trusting only a farmer's eyes, a photo app built in Tainan can now spot disease across ten separate crops. It catches problems well before serious damage actually spreads.
slides.11: Scientists working in Tainan have also been breeding sturdier crop varieties since 1971. That project still helps feed people both here in Taiwan and much farther away too.
slides.12: However, there's a catch that rarely gets mentioned. Taiwan still won't allow genetically modified crops to be grown on its own soil, even though it freely imports modified grain to feed livestock.
slides.13: Every single LED light draws genuine electricity, and that expense builds up surprisingly fast. Lighting alone can account for roughly half of a brand-new indoor farm's entire setup cost.
slides.14: If no state support ever shows up, that steep power bill just keeps climbing regardless. Vegetables grown indoors often cost more than the same vegetable grown outdoors in a nearby field.
slides.15: Aquaculture faces a similar squeeze. Skilled techniques for raising grouper have made their way across the strait to rival operations, and export money has fallen by roughly three billion dollars.
slides.16: So the hardest part was clearly never inventing this. The real difficulty Taiwan continues confronting is making it cheap enough, legal enough, and safe from ever being copied.
slides.17: Put simply, Taiwan has already built real farm technology, well beyond a lab test or a tiny trial. Genetics research, LED growing racks and smart sensors now operate side by side.
slides.18: Closing this gap will take real engineering, biology, and data skills working together, not luck. That combination of skills could easily describe several people in this very room.
slides.19: So here's a question worth asking. What could a cheaper LED, a faster sensor, or a better-protected idea actually do for a farmer who truly has no successor?
slides.20: This unusual growing space could genuinely become tomorrow's normal farm, so let's shape that whole future carefully. Nobody wants to wait until the very last farmer quietly disappears.
